Mike Rogers and his second wife, Kristi, saw their wealth rise substantially
after Rogers was elevated to chair of the House Intelligence Committee in 2011
and lucrative government contracts poured her way, a review of financial
disclosures finds.

Rogers was first elected to Congress in 2000, in time to be a major backer of
the Iraq war. With a background at the FBI, Rogers was encouraged by Speaker
Dennis Hastert to get involved in foreign policy and national security
matters. According to the [Rogers Archive at Oakland
University,](https://library.oakland.edu/MikeRogers/people.html) he made seven
trips to Iraq between 2001 and 2005 as a member of Congress. In 2005, he was
appointed to the House Intelligence Committee. (Drop Site could not
independently verify the number of trips, but taking seven trips to Iraq in
the space of four years would be highly unusual for a member of Congress--and
trips in 2001 or 2002, before the invasion, are unlikely.)

Kristi Clemens was a top press aide to L. Paul Bremer, who oversaw the U.S.
occupation of Iraq as head of the Coalition Provisional Authority. Clemens
turned heads in DC in 2006, when, following her role in Iraq, she successfully
pitched the major British security contractor Aegis Defence Services to launch
an American offshoot. Within three years, she rose to CEO and president.
Rogers divorced his wife of 17 years in 2007 and married Clemens in 2010. By
2011, when Mike Rogers assumed his chairmanship, she was vice chair of Aegis
LLC US.

After his divorce, according to Rogers's financial disclosures, the
congressman had few assets to his name and little wealth. That would soon
change.

The Rogers family added at least hundreds of thousands of dollars to their net
worth as Rogers was elevated to chair of the House Permanent Select Committee
on Intelligence (HPSCI) and Kristi Rogers's private military security company
received increasingly large contracts from the U.S. government, according to
Rogers's financial disclosures. The couple added millions more after Rogers
left the House and began working in the industry he had spent years
overseeing.

While Rogers is not required to disclose his spouse's income, their reported
"Unearned Income," including multiple investment funds, dividends, and
interest income, soared over those years. They also acquired two mortgages in
Maryland and Virginia--neither principal residences.

In 2010, Aegis was named one of only eight private military contractors who
were qualified to bid on $10 billion of contracts for the State Department's
Worldwide Protection (WWP) program. The biggest fish, the Kabul Afghanistan
Embassy Security contract, first went to another firm but was re-competed and
awarded to Aegis LLC.

Kristi Rogers claimed credit for this in a biography later scrubbed from the
website of the law firm Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, which stated she led "a
two-year pursuit and capture strategy to win a five-year, $10 billion
contract." Mike Rogers was appointed Chairman on January 3, 2011; the contract
was awarded to Aegis seven months later, on July 29th, 2011.

## **From Opioids to Intel**

Mike Rogers [spent his first eight years in
Congress](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/mike-rogers-senate-opioids-oxycontin)
as a lead advocate for the opioid industry in Congress, but as the resulting
epidemic surged and his longtime patrons came under federal investigation, he
pivoted fully to national security following the Tea Party wave of 2010 that
swept Republicans to power.

As chair of HPSCI, Rogers had access to sensitive and top secret intelligence
that is unavailable to rank-and-file lawmakers, and the position is one of the
most powerful in Washington. (Technically, the Appropriations Committee is
supposed to have more power over spending decisions in Congress, but
legislation now is generally adopted through a so-called "continuing
resolution" or an omnibus spending package, bypassing regular order.)

In 2007, Rogers got into a public battle with then-Rep. Jack Murtha (D-Penn.)
when Rogers attempted to defund the National Intelligence Drug Center, based
in Murtha's district. Rogers [argued the
money](https://www.congress.gov/110/crec/2007/05/21/CREC-2007-05-21.pdf)
"takes precious intelligence resources from spies on the ground catching
terrorists in places like Fallujah, Iraq, and sends it to bureaucrats in
Johnstown, Pennsylvania." Aegis, of course, was a leading provider of security
contracting in Iraq at the time.

Rogers and his wife rose in tandem. By her own account in Washington Exec,
Kristi Clemens[ in 2006 made a pitch to start the U.S. branch of Aegis Defence
Ltd](https://washingtonexec.com/exec-profiles/now-kristi-rogers), to the
company's board, which included a 5-Star UK Colonel and Winston Churchill's
grandson. It's not clear whether he and Clemens had met yet. The company made
her executive vice president, then president in 2008, chief executive in 2009,
president in 2010, and vice chairman in 2011.

Aegis, a UK private military contractor, was founded by Tim Spicer, a
controversial figure thanks to three international scandals involving his
first company, Sandline. The Nation [reported in
2004](https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/tim-spicers-world/) that
Spicer had been caught "violating a UN Arms embargo in Sierra Leone and
unwittingly triggering a coup in Papua New Guinea," prompting its military to
arrest Spicer. They found $400,000 in cash on him. It was a surprise to many
in Iraq and D.C. that Spicer's new firm, Aegis Defence Services,[ landed a
major $293 million Pentagon
contract](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JgwUfdiFOFM) in 2004 to protect U.S.
diplomats in Iraq. Five Democratic U.S. senators, led by Ted Kennedy, appealed
to Secretary of State Donald Rumsfeld to reconsider the award based on
Spicer's scandals, but were rebuffed. By 2007, with Kristi Rogers in place at
Aegis U.S.,[ the largest single contract--for $475 million
dollars](https://www.securityworldmarket.com/uk/Newsarchive/aegis-wins-
usd475-million-contract-renewal-for-iraq)--was awarded to Aegis by the Defense
Department; it included supporting the Army Corps of Engineers in
reconstruction operations in Iraq.

The 2004 contract made Aegis head of the regional operating centers and later
the Contractor Operations Cell (CONOC), responsible for providing situational
awareness and coordinating the movements of private security contractors. That
put Aegis in charge of coordination of all the other private military
contractors in Iraq, earning Aegis's Spicer the moniker of[ "the general in
charge of all of the private
contractors,"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JgwUfdiFOFM)

Under Aegis ostensible oversight, Blackwater contractors were involved in the
2007 Nisour Square massacre, in which 17 innocent Iraqi civilians were killed.
In 2005, [Aegis drew international attention
](https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna10400255)when one of their gunmen posted a
video of their vehicle wildly shooting at civilian vehicles en route from the
Green Zone to the airport, set to the Elvis song, "Mystery Train." At least
one civilian was reported killed.

None of it stopped the company's rise. Aegis was awarded the Armed Contractor
Oversight Directorate, or ACOD, contract in 2009 for Afghanistan, which
oversees contractors. That produced a glaring conflict of interest--overseeing
other contractors while also bidding against them--and one former ACOD
whistleblower ordered what's called a "Cure Notice," effectively calling out a
conflict-of-interest and demanding it be fixed.

A congressional commission set up to root out waste and fraud in wartime
contracting called Kristi Rogers to testify, but she begged off, citing her
honeymoon in spring 2010. One commissioner at the hearing noted that he
understood her board had advised her not to attend.

That summer, [on June 21, 2010, she testified as Aegis's
president.](https://www.c-span.org/program/public-affairs-event/wartime-
contracts-and-private-security-firms-executives-panel/226672) Commissioner
Charles Tiefer put it to her that Aegis personnel "currently operate the CONOC
[the center coordinating other armed contractors] in Iraq." "We support it,
yes," she said.

Kristi Rogers said the whistleblower who had flagged the conflicts of interest
was a "disgruntled former employee," but she admitted the company was forced
to terminate its ACOD duties.

Despite the scandals, 20 months later, Aegis landed that $1.017 billion
contract to secure the Kabul, Afghanistan Embassy. .

The pursuit of further contracts took Aegis to Libya, where NATO intervention
had produced widespread violence with the overthrow of Moamar Gaddafi. Aegis
had an intelligence arm called Aegis Advisory Services, in Libya, with a large
team in Tripoli that boasted of top security clearance status, and clients
which included the world's elite private intelligence group, Stratfor.

In September 2012, a U.S. compound in Benghazi was sacked, killing four
Americans: two private contractors, the U.S. ambassador to Libya, and a State
Department official. Al Jazeera later reported that Aegis had been bidding for
a $5 billion contract to secure all of Libya's porous borders. In 2014, the
conservative group Judicial Watch, relying in part on documents published by
WikiLeaks, found that Aegis had been heavily active in Libya since early 2011
and that it had assessed Benghazi in the summer before the attack.

## **After Benghazi**

Republicans spent years investigating the lapses and policy decisions that led
to the fatal attack, while Kristi Rogers and her company were walled off from
the Intelligence Committee, a spokesperson said at the time. Through its
spokesperson Susan Phalan, HPSCI announced a "no interaction policy with Mrs.
Rogers or any Aegis employee." (The no interaction policy presumably did not
apply between husband and wife.)

Judicial Watch's Micah Morrison [was unsparing
](https://dailycaller.com/2014/06/17/unraveling-benghazi-is-mike-rogers-part-
of-the-problem/)in its criticism of Rogers in a report headlined "Unraveling
Benghazi: Is Mike Rogers Part of the Problem?":

> Sussing out the White House's response to Benghazi is a critical step in
> clearing the shadows from the incident, but there are other players in the
> drama as well, including Rep. Rogers, and possibly also including a private
> military contracting firm that until recently was run by his wife, Kristi
> Rogers. Mike and Kristi Rogers are quintessential Washington insiders. A
> seven-term Republican from Michigan, Mike Rogers climbed the political
> ladder to become chairman of the Intelligence Committee in January 2011.
> Kristi Rogers, after years of government service in mid-level administrative
> positions, moved to the private sector, joining the British-based security
> contractor Aegis Defense Services to help open its U.S. subsidiary. The
> newsletter Intelligence Online noted that thanks to Ms. Rogers' efforts,
> "Aegis won several major contracts with the U.S. administration."
>
> A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee noted that "strictly
> observed and enforced" policies required "that there should be no
> interaction with Mrs. Rogers on any matter relating to the official business
> of the House" and "no interaction between the Committee and any
> representative of Aegis." There is no evidence of wrong-doing by Rep. Rogers
> or Aegis. Indeed, the outlines of the story are more suggestive of "right-
> doing," Washington-style: an insider's game of covert operations and
> corporate profits played out in the gray areas of law and policy.

That spring--though, as Judicial Watch noted, there was no direct evidence of
criminal wrongdoing--Rogers announced he would not be running for re-election,
and his wife left Aegis. Rogers went into corporate and cyber security work,
and was floated as CIA director in the first Trump administration.

Leading right-wing pollster and operative Dick Morris, who had questioned Mike
Rogers's oversight of Benghazi, wanted to make sure that conservatives never
forgot about his work. Rogers had fought the formation of a special committee
to investigate it, and conservatives believed he was slow-walking the probe to
protect his wife's company. "The first to go--and most deserving--is former
Congressman and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Mike Rogers," Morris
[wrote](https://www.dickmorris.com/bravo-pence-ousts-mike-rogers-dick-morris-
tv-lunch-alert/). "Slated, some say, to be the new director of the CIA, Rogers
was a key force in obstructing and delaying the Benghazi investigation in
order to shield his wife, Kristi, from scrutiny."

Morris went on: "Aegis had won several major contracts, likely through Mrs.
Rogers' influence as the wife of the House Intel Committee. Although not
directly responsible for security at Benghazi, her firm had significant
responsibilities in the area."

The late Sen. Lindsey Graham called the HPSCI report on Benghazi[ "full of
crap,"](https://www.cnn.com/2014/11/23/politics/lindsey-graham-benghazi-
report) while former U.S. Attorney Joe DiGenova [went on WMAL Radio in D.C.
](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YEHFuiXnVJU)during the hearings and accused
Mike Rogers of "sabotaging the Benghazi hearings" and went so far as to warn
future Republicans to pay attention to the "dishonorable conduct of Mike
Rogers."

Judicial Watch's Micah Morrison called the couple the "quintessential
Washington insiders." In November 2012, the Rogers family took a six-day, all-
expenses-paid trip to Buenos Aires, Argentina, costing its sponsors, the
Franklin Center and the Ripon Center, $23,540.

Rogers announced his departure on the Paul W. Smith morning drive show on WJR
Radio in Detroit on March 28, 2014, saying that he would finish his term and
become a talk radio host on Cumulus Radio, WJR's syndicator. On the show,
Rogers said he always believed in "a citizen legislature," that he had a
private-sector career before his public service, and that he intended to
return to one.

After his years spent regulating the surveillance industry as chair of the
Intelligence Committee, Rogers began working with multiple cybersecurity
companies.

Rogers ran unsuccessfully for the Michigan Senate in 2024 and is running again
in 2026. His Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, [has repeatedly attacked
him](https://bridgemi.com/michigan-government/fact-check-abdul-el-sayed-and-
mike-rogers-debate-trump-tariffs-war-more/) for making up to $14 million in
the private sector from the types of companies he was tasked with regulating.

Rogers has insisted that his work in Congress and his wife's work as head of
Aegis U.S. were kept separate. When reached for comment, the campaign said:
"The accusation that Mike used his position in Congress to protect his family
in any way, shape, or form is patently false. If you want to talk about
families, let's talk about Abdul El-Sayed's father-in-law serving on the board
of CAIR while funding his Senate race. Abdul is alarmingly close to designated
terrorist organizations, and Michigan must be protected from him at all
costs." (CAIR--the Council on American-Islamic Relations--is not a designated
terrorist organization.)
